content: The May 1, 2014, updates to the HIV treatment guidelines introduced significant changes to existing sections and added two new tables. These updates include the following: 1. Recommended Regimens for ART-Naïve Patients: There are now five recommended regimens for antiretroviral therapy (ART)-naïve patients. Four of these are based on integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs), and one is based on a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor (PI/r). INSTI-Based Regimens: Dolutegravir/abacavir/lamivudine (DTG/ABC/3TC) is recommended only for patients who are HLA-B5701 negative (AI). Dolutegravir plus tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine (DTG + TDF/FTC) is recommended (AI). Elvitegravir/cobicistat/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine (EVG/c/TDF/FTC) is recommended only for patients with pre-ART creatinine clearance (CrCl) >70 mL/min (AI). Raltegravir (RAL) plus TDF/FTC is recommended (AI). PI/r-Based Regimen: Darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r) plus TDF/FTC is recommended (AI). 2. Changes to Previously Recommended Regimens: Two regimens previously classified as Recommended have been moved to the Alternative category: Atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r) plus TDF/FTC (BI): This change is based on a large clinical trial showing higher rates of discontinuation due to toxicities compared to DRV/r or RAL plus TDF/FTC. Efavirenz/TDF/FTC (EFV/TDF/FTC) (BI): This change is due to concerns about EFV tolerability, particularly central nervous system (CNS)-related toxicities and a potential association with suicidality. Three regimens (ATV/r + ABC/3TC, EFV + ABC/3TC, and rilpivirine/TDF/FTC) previously listed as Recommended for patients with baseline HIV RNA <100,000 copies/mL or CD4 counts >200 cells/mm³ are now in the Alternative or Other categories, with the same caveats about their use in these populations. Two regimens using fewer than two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs)—DRV/r + RAL and lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) + 3TC—are now listed under Other regimens. Their use is limited to patients who cannot take either TDF or ABC. Coformulations of atazanavir (ATV) and darunavir (DRV) with the pharmacokinetic enhancer cobicistat (COBI) have been added to the Alternative regimen options. 3. Virologic Failure: The section on managing virologic failure in different clinical scenarios has been expanded to include guidance for patients failing firstand second-line ART regimens. A new subsection on isolated CNS virologic failure and new-onset neurologic symptoms has been added. The subsection on suboptimal immunologic response despite viral suppression has been moved to a standalone section. 4. Advances in ART: Since the advent of potent combination therapy in 1996, ART has steadily improved. New drugs with novel mechanisms of action, enhanced potency, activity against multidrug-resistant viruses, improved dosing convenience, and better tolerability have been approved. ART has significantly reduced HIV-associated morbidity and mortality, transforming HIV into a chronic, manageable condition. Effective ART also prevents transmission to sexual partners. Despite these advances, less than one-third of HIV-infected individuals in the U.S. have suppressed viral loads, primarily due to undiagnosed infections and failure to link or retain diagnosed patients in care. Economic and social barriers continue to contribute to morbidity, mortality, and new infections. 5. Guideline Development and Updates: The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Panel on Antiretroviral Guidelines for Adults and Adolescents, a working group of the Office of AIDS Research Advisory Council (OARAC), provides recommendations based on current knowledge of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs for treating HIV in adults and adolescents in the U.S. The Panel reviews new evidence and updates recommendations as needed. These guidelines represent the state of knowledge regarding ARV use but may not always align with FDA-approved labeling or legal standards for product approval. Clinicians are encouraged to exercise clinical judgment tailored to individual patient circumstances and to participate in well-designed, IRB-approved clinical trials to address unanswered questions about ART safety and efficacy. 6. Baseline Evaluation: Every HIV-infected patient entering care should undergo a comprehensive medical history, physical examination, laboratory evaluation, and counseling about the implications of HIV infection. The goals of the initial evaluation include confirming the HIV diagnosis, obtaining baseline historical and laboratory data, ensuring patient understanding of HIV and its transmission, and initiating care as recommended in HIV primary care and opportunistic infection guidelines. Baseline laboratory tests include HIV antibody testing, CD4 T-cell count, plasma HIV RNA (viral load), complete blood count, chemistry profile, transaminase levels, renal function tests, fasting glucose, lipid profile, and genotypic resistance testing. Additional tests for sexually transmitted infections and opportunistic infection risk should be performed as needed. 7. Monitoring ART Response: Viral load and CD4 count are the primary markers for monitoring ART response and disease progression. Viral load is the most important indicator of ART effectiveness and should be measured at entry into care, at therapy initiation, and regularly thereafter. Optimal viral suppression is defined as a viral load persistently below the level of detection. CD4 count provides information on immune function and is critical for determining the need for opportunistic infection prophylaxis and assessing the urgency of ART initiation. Frequent CD4 monitoring is unnecessary for virologically suppressed patients with stable immune reconstitution. 8. Drug-Resistance Testing: Genotypic and phenotypic resistance assays are used to assess viral strains and guide treatment strategies. Genotypic assays detect drug-resistance mutations in relevant viral genes and are the preferred method for resistance testing in ART-naïve patients. Resistance testing is recommended at entry into care, regardless of whether ART will be initiated immediately or deferred. If therapy is deferred, repeat testing should be considered at the time of ART initiation. These updates reflect the evolving science of HIV treatment and emphasize the importance of individualized care, adherence to therapy, and addressing barriers to effective treatment and prevention.
